clue.text: One may produce a portion of quiche, for example

definitions.text: One may produce a portion of quiche, for example

indicators.note: a portion is a part, so the answer is a stretch of letters taken from inside the words quiche, for

explanation.surface: A cook is credited with making slices of a savoury tart.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'quiche, for'; read as a whole, the clue also describes the person who makes quiche.
explanation.definitionFit: A cook in a restaurant kitchen is the person who produces dishes such as quiche.

clue.text: Government scheme for picking one out of the pack

definitions.text: Government scheme for picking one out of the pack

parts.words: Government scheme for picking one out of the pack
parts.note: a state plan for documents that single out a person from the crowd, read playfully as choosing one from a deck

explanation.surface: An official plan for identifying an individual among a crowd of citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' suggests a deck of playing cards, nodding to the second word, while the scheme was the UK's proposed national documents.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK government proposed a national scheme of personal documents proving who a citizen is.

clue.text: 24 with no exercise becomes a pudding

indicators.note: with no means the following thing is taken away from the first word

parts.note: the answer to 24-down, an old skin disease
PE is physical exercise, as in school PE lessons

explanation.surface: Something without any workout turns into a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no' removes PE from SAPEGO, the 24-down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Starchy grains from a palm are cooked with milk to make a classic British milk pudding.

clue.text: What fell off a lorry with a direct hit?

parts.note: stuff said to have fallen off a lorry is merchandise, i.e. goods
the phrase is British slang for stolen, and stolen items are called hot

explanation.surface: A question about stolen merchandise linked to a precise strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell off the back of a lorry' is British slang for stolen goods; the surface reads as a question about crime, but the phrase supplies both halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise for an accurate strike on a target, especially in shooting or ball games.

clue.text: Establishment only designed for old colony

parts.note: the Church of England, abbreviated CE, is the established church

indicators.note: something designed is arranged or worked out afresh, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An institution built purely for a former territory of the empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Designed' rearranges the word only; 'Establishment' points to the Church of England as the Established Church.
explanation.definitionFit: Sri Lanka was the British colony formerly known by this name until 1972.

clue.text: Worry about fellow, one unable to cope

annotationWithheld.why: Worry about fellow, one unable to cope (3,7): BADGER around MAN + A needs 'one' for A, but 'one' is also needed in the definition 'one unable to cope'; the word does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Worry about fellow, one unable to cope

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd or peculiar, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the name Milne with its S counted as a letter

explanation.surface: A man named Lambert owns a cake made by a writer called Milne that is comical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lambert' points to Lambert Simnel, the 15th-century pretender to the English throne, supporting the answer as a name; 'funny' rearranges MILNES.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit cake with marzipan, traditionally eaten in Britain at Easter or on Mothering Sunday.

indicators.note: a nose out of joint is put out, and dislocated letters get rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 29-down, a facial feature

explanation.surface: People find someone's nose put out of joint, upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of joint' rearranges NOSE, the 29-down answer; the surface plays on the idiom for being offended.
explanation.definitionFit: Single people or units can each be called an individual, as in 'little ones'.

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A beast appears in a book by Thomas Hardy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy novel' tempts a hunt through Hardy's titles; 'novel' rearranges HARDY.
explanation.definitionFit: The many-headed serpent of Greek myth killed by Heracles.

indicators.note: in places the word for proportion inside the word open

parts.note: taken as written
a ratio is a proportion between quantities

explanation.surface: A balance found in an open-plan clinic.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical procedure carried out on a patient is an operation.

clue.text: It's amusing to go and get laid, possibly like a mushroom

parts.note: something amusing is fun
taken as written

indicators.note: possibly means the letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it a laugh to go off and sleep with someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges laid; 'It's' and 'and get' are link words in a racy surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things resembling a fungus, of which a mushroom is an example.

clue.text: In sum, it might be less

definitions.text: In sum, it might be less

parts.words: In sum, it might be less
parts.note: in arithmetic the subtracting sign means taking away, so a total becomes smaller

explanation.surface: In short, it might be fewer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In sum' looks like 'in summary', but it means within an arithmetic calculation.
explanation.definitionFit: The subtraction sign in a sum signals that one quantity is taken away, leaving less.

indicators.note: play suggests the letters are moved about freely

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, 'that is'
the word child, the possessive giving no letter

explanation.surface: A casual party that is easy as child's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' gives IE and 'play' rearranges IE with CHILD.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish or Irish social gathering with folk music and dancing is an informal party.

clue.text: Depict the Italian prevalence of sin?

parts.note: il is the Italian for 'the'
lust is one of the seven deadly sins
a rate is how common something is

explanation.surface: Show how common wrongdoing is among Italians.
explanation.definitionFit: To portray something in pictures or examples is to depict it.

definitions.meaning: the 12-across answer, a subtraction sign, is the opposite of plus, i.e. not plus

explanation.walkthrough: 12-across is MINUS; its sense 'not plus' is spelt out, in Latin-flavoured form, as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at a loss about what to do is to be in bewilderment or perplexity.

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of musical

explanation.surface: A playwright's debut stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatist's first musical' reads as a work, but it splits into SHAW and the first letter of 'musical'.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval double-reed wind instrument, a forerunner of the oboe.

parts.note: Roy is a boy's name
Al is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A pair of lads with links to Windsor.
explanation.walkthrough: Windsor is the British royal family's name and castle.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Windsor is the British monarch's family, so belonging to it is regal.

indicators.note: a return sends the word back, so it is read backwards

parts.note: Postman Pat is a British children's TV postman

explanation.surface: The postman comes back and raps at the door.
explanation.walkthrough: Postman Pat is a British children's TV character.
explanation.definitionFit: A light rap or knock on a door or surface.

definitions.meaning: to woo or court someone romantically
whimsically, a court that rules on wage disputes

explanation.walkthrough: An industrial tribunal hears employment disputes, often over wages, so the question mark invites reading it as a court for wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooing someone means making romantic advances to them.

clue.text: Reptile unknown out of South American country

indicators.note: out of means the unknown letter is removed from the country

parts.note: Guyana is a country on South America's north coast
y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: An unidentified lizard gets out of a South American nation.
explanation.definitionFit: An older name for the iguana, a large tropical lizard.

clue.text: Hood taking a gun, inspiring terror

parts.note: a hood is a hoodlum, such as Al Capone
arming oneself is taking up a weapon

explanation.surface: A gangster picks up a weapon, frightening everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hood' suggests a garment, but it is a gangster: Al Capone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that causes fear or alarm is frightening.

parts.note: sin is wickedness
uses are purposes things serve

explanation.surface: Holes intended for wicked ends.
explanation.definitionFit: The hollow air-filled spaces in the skull bones are cavities.

definitions.meaning: Charles Pooter writes The Diary of a ... by George and Weedon Grossmith

explanation.walkthrough: The Diary of a Nobody is a classic English comic novel; split, the answer also means without a body.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional Mr Pooter's diary is titled as that of an insignificant person.

clue.text: Old skin disease liable to drain confidence

parts.note: to sap is to drain strength
ego is self-esteem

explanation.surface: An outdated rash that may undermine self-belief.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic name for a scaly skin eruption, such as eczema.

clue.text: The law's reach extending to maritime equipment

parts.note: Scotland Yard, the Metropolitan Police, is the law
the long arm of the law is its reach

explanation.surface: The authorities' reach stretches as far as ships.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's police.
explanation.definitionFit: Either end of a ship's yard, the spar holding a sail, is a part of maritime rigging.

indicators.note: rotten implies decay, so the letters break down and rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone called Murphy is denounced as a nasty brute.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy is slang for a potato, from the Irish surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato is a swollen underground stem, an example of a tuber.

indicators.note: half takes the first four of the eight letters of thorough

explanation.surface: A deity is truly thorough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't half' is British slang for 'very', but here 'half' takes the first half of 'thorough'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse god of thunder.

clue.text: Poland has enough, possibly about 1,000 farm workers

parts.note: PL is the international code for Poland

indicators.note: about means the anagram surrounds the thousand
possibly means the letters might be rearranged

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for 1,000

explanation.surface: Poland may have about a thousand agricultural labourers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges ENOUGH into OUGHEN and 'about' puts M inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Labourers who till fields with a plough are farm workers.
Heaving as if to vomit, and also jokes in a comic's routine.

indicators.note: in places the mapmakers within the region

parts.note: Northumberland lies in the North East of England, NE
OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's map-maker

explanation.surface: A characteristic of mapmakers in northern England.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ordnance Survey is Britain's national mapping agency.
explanation.definitionFit: A facial feature is a part of the face, the nose being one.

indicators.note: a product is something made, so these letters are remade

explanation.surface: A veteran sold a wonderful item.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran with long experience is an old hand.

indicators.note: missing means the one is left out of the word

parts.note: a genius is a brilliant, inspired person
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A brilliant person lacks something.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology a genus is a classification rank, a class of related species.
